#19 [paper] Global Ocean Observing System status Report 2026
Authors: M. Belbéoch, Z. Begg, S. Fournier, N. Kolodziejczyk, Joanna Post, Bipendra Prakash, E. Rusciano, Laura Stukonytė
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0bd03e1cb89a8bcbb96b251c54aebf44383502c3
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a comprehensive overview of the status, coverage, and sustainability of the global ocean observing system, including gaps in capacity and funding.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Compilation of an interactive status report aggregating statistics on national contributions, monitoring data from 17 GOOS observing networks via OceanOPS, satellite observations, and data from marine life initiatives, supplemented by qualitative impact stories.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observations from the seafloor to the atmosphere, involving 67 countries, 17 GOOS observing networks, satellite systems, and diverse marine ecosystem initiatives.
Abstract:
The ocean underpins the safety, wellbeing and livelihoods of communities worldwide. Understanding how it is changing depends on sustained ocean observations: the measurements collected by dedicated people, instruments and platforms, from the seafloor to the atmosphere. The Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) Status Report 2026 provides an interactive overview of the status of the global ocean observing system, presents new statistics on national contributions, and showcases the societal value of ocean observations through impact stories from around the globe. Today, 67 countries contribute to physical and biogeochemical ocean observations at sea through 17 GOOS observing networks monitored by OceanOPS. Satellites complement these measurements with observations from space, while a diverse community of initiatives collects vital data on marine life and ecosystems. Together, these observations underpin weather forecasting, climate monitoring, maritime and coastal risk management, biodiversity conservation and sustainable ocean economies. The global ocean observing system continues to make progress, supported by established observing networks, long-term reference observatories, regional systems and emerging technologies. Yet, important gaps and risks remain. Observing capacity is unevenly distributed around the world, and many networks face challenges in securing the sustained funding needed to maintain and expand their observations. Strengthening coordination, improving data sharing and broadening international participation will be essential to build a more comprehensive, resilient and sustainable system. Continued investment and stronger collaboration across countries and observing communities are crucial to ensure that ocean observations can meet growing scientific, operational and societal needs. Explore the interactive GOOS Status Report to find out more.

#21 [paper] Designing optimal biodiversity observation networks
Authors: Michael Catchen, Francis Banville, Penelope Blyth, Chris Brimacombe, Gabriel Dansereau, Gracielle Higino, Thomas Malpas, Hana Mayall
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.32942/x22t28
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Meeting the goals of the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) requires a substantial increase in biodiversity monitoring effort, motivating the development of a Global Biodiversity Observing System (GBiOS). However, GBiOS cannot be built without a practical framework for designing effective biodiversity monitoring networks that balances budgetary constraints with competing policy objectives, which we currently lack. Here we provide the foundations for a theory of optimal biodiversity monitoring design based on: (1) a hierarchical, multi-layer architecture for monitoring networks that matches the multi-scale nature of ecological processes and environmental policymaking, (2) a simulation-based framework for evaluating the efficacy of monitoring network design against the variety of plausible “ecological worlds”, and (3) an integrative toolbox for monitoring design, drawing on methods from spatial sampling theory, environmental monitoring design, and optimal decision theory. Together, these form a basis for building the most effective GBiOS possible to best inform policymaking and meet the goals and targets of the GBF.

#27 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

results.content:
#32 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

final_text:
Here's what I found, and where I hit a wall.

## Best fit: #20 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)

Of the open grants in the Plastic pathways slate, #20 is the strongest fit. The project's declared concepts — marine litter tracking, satellite ocean remote sensing, floating debris detection, Lagrangian particle tracking, beaching — map directly onto #20's aim to strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system, including closing structural gaps in under-observed regions. The project's satellite-based debris detection work is a natural contribution to the observing-capacity and data-coordination goals #20 asks for.

The biggest doubt: #20 is a €50M flagship call centred on GOOS governance, deep-sea and polar gaps, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. The project's plastic-pathways focus is a component of that, not its centre — the proposal would need to frame debris observation as part of a broader observing-system story, and the call explicitly asks for industry partners and GOOS governance engagement, which the project's current scope doesn't cover.

The other open grants in the slate fit less well:
- **#32 Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination** (NSF, deadline 2027-02-15) is about instrumentation development with broad applicability — a possible angle if the project builds new debris-detection instruments, but that's not what the project currently declares.
- **#23 Green, circular and resilient harbours** and **#33 Coastal resilience** (both deadline 2027-09-21) are place-based Mission calls requiring port authorities or public administrations as partners and demonstrations in at least 4 ports or 6 sites. They touch pollution but are not about plastic pathways.
- **#4 Microplastics Research and Resource Coordination Center** (deadline 2026-12-01) is biomedical — health effects of micro/nanoplastics, sampling standardisation. Different field from the project's environmental pathways work.

## Who in the lab should lead

For #20, the evidence points to **Priya Raman (#16)** as lead: her declared satellite ocean remote sensing profile is the closest match to the call's observing-capacity requirements, and the nightly ranking placed her first. **You (#14)** are the second name — your declared data-assimilation-with-ML profile supports the call's data-delivery and forecasting-resilience goals.

One honest caveat: the ranking matched people to the call's *general* observing-system slots, not specifically to the plastic-pathways angle. No one in the lab declares floating debris detection or Lagrangian particle tracking — those are project concepts currently held by no member's profile. If the proposal leans on the debris-detection method, that's a gap to close either by updating a profile or by naming the person who actually does that work.

## Who outside the lab

I could not finish this part. Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I have no consented outside-lab suggestions to offer. What I can say from the call's text: #20 explicitly expects partners from marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, and it asks for engagement with GOOS/IOC-UNESCO governance frameworks. Those are the partner types the proposal would need. If you turn on collaborator search, I can check who in the wider network has consented and matches those slots.

## What I could not finish

- I could not read the project's full confirmed state (problem, method, milestones) — the project record only returned its name and members. The fit assessment above is based on the project's declared concepts and its slate, not a full project read.
- The outside-lab partner question is blocked by the collaborator search being off, as noted above.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-03
Still open/current: yes

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- environment and society at large benefit from recyclable plastic products which can be recycled back into high value applications;

- industrial value chains introduce circular plastic products on the market through enhanced design for recycling and solutions for effective sorting and recycling on a large scale;

- industrial value chains are equipped with improved characterisation of waste from complex plastic materials to enable its recycling.

Scope:

The topic supports the European Green Deal, the Regulation on Packaging and Packaging Waste, the Waste Shipment Regulation, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, the upcoming Circular Economy Act and contributes to Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products. It also contributes to the new EU bioeconomy strategy, the Life Sciences Strategy and the EU Biotech Act and is relevant to the European Commission’s communication: ‘Building the future with nature: Boosting Biotechnology and Biomanufacturing in the EU’.

Proposals should:

- advance novel biotech solutions for recycling of complex plastic materials and products (multi-material/multi-layer/composites), namely in the sectors of packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure and transport;

- propose recommendations towards fit-for-purpose regulatory risk assessments for novel materials and recycling technologies (i.e. hazard identification, methodological updates) and take into account the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework;

- consider the latest solutions in material innovation while developing novel recycling solutions e.g. by application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced degradation of plastics;

- demonstrate the solutions on a pilot scale involving the whole value chain.

Successful proposals are expected to evaluate the feasibility, effectiveness and impact of the demonstrated solutions using robust evaluation methods (including lifecycle assessments such as product environmental footprint, where relevant) and present data and evidence about the economic, environmental and social costs and benefits of the developed solutions.

Industrial value chains are expected to take part in the proposed consortia to enable a demonstration of the proposed solution and involve all relevant stakeholders.

Clustering with other relevant Horizon Europe projects is encouraged.

#10 [grant] Innovative Solutions for mitigating the environmental impact of waterborne transport in marine and aquatic Ecosystems (ZEWT Partnership)
Amount: €2,000,000–€13,500,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-03-D5-17
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

Here's the corrected summary for **Plastic pathways**.

## Where the project stands

The project is a lab project with three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. Its confirmed state (goals, method, blockers, stage, milestones) isn't visible to me right now, so I can't confirm how far along it is or what's blocking it. If the state was set more than thirty days ago it may be out of date — you can update it in the app.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week:

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-point: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. If your project tracks how plastic moves and where it ends up, this is a ready-made method and codebase to build on.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Relevant as a template for the satellite side: a YOLO11-based framework (YOLO11-ISW) for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation of low-contrast, curved features in MODIS imagery, applied to imagery from 2011 to 2020. The same approach could be adapted to detect plastic accumulations or debris plumes from space.

3. **#11 — "Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array."** Less directly about plastic, but it's a good example of turning a sparse in-situ float network into basin-scale trends — useful if part of your pathway work involves reconciling field sampling with broader ocean context.

## One funding opportunity

**#12 — "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework"** (Horizon Europe, €3–8M, deadline 22 Sep 2027). It calls for multisensory data-integration systems that harmonise in-situ observations with satellite remote sensing and AI analytics, with marine demonstration cases in ecosystems under pressure. Plastic pathways — field records plus satellite observation of debris — fits that shape well, and the deadline gives you a full year to shape a proposal.

A runner-up worth noting: **#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System"** (€50M, deadline 16 Feb 2027) is a much bigger, infrastructure-level call; it would suit the project only if you can frame it as contributing to a broader observing network rather than a single study.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's current state and blockers in the app so I can tie the slate to what's actually holding you up, and take a closer look at #6's code — it may save the team months of kernel development.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

The one that matters most is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Why it stands out for this project:

- **It's the proof of concept you're building toward.** Your project is about *early warning* — the value of a heatwave forecast only exists if it changes what people do. #4 is a documented case where a forecast ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño triggered an expert workshop, which triggered a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish before in-situ temperatures broke records (80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature). That's the full loop: forecast → decision → action → survival confirmed after release.
- **It's the strongest argument for your project's existence.** When you're justifying the early-warning system to funders or coastal managers, this is the concrete example that a forecast can buy real time for a threatened species.
- **It's new on the slate** (entered 2026-11-10), so it's fresh ammunition.

The runner-up is **#5 — the 1–14-day ML marine heatwave forecast evaluation in the Northern Bay of Bengal**, which is the closest methodological match to your ML-for-data-assimilation interest and directly relevant to short-range MHW forecast skill. But it's a thesis code/data release (Zenodo, 2026) with a thin abstract, so it's more of a methods reference than a story.

**#3** (the seasonal Northeast Pacific ocean forecast system) is also strong — 32-year retrospective evaluation, ACC > 0.5 at multi-month leads, and routine real-time forecasts starting October 2026 — but it's a comment/review of an existing system rather than a new result, and its seasonal timescale is a step removed from your early-warning focus.

If I had to pick one to read first: **#4**, because it turns your project's output (a forecast) into a narrative about survival, which is what makes early warning matter.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

The clearest fit is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:

- **It is the only item on the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The rest touch the ocean only indirectly — phytoplankton production (#3, #9), a forecast system (#5), internal waves (#7), a turtle habitat study (#12), and so on.
- **It is a methods paper, not just a result.** It ships a three-phase *beaching kernel* plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated results behind every number in the manuscript. That is a ready-made component for modelling how plastic reaches shore — the "pathways" part of your project.
- **It is validated against field records** (beaching observations from Uido, Korea, driven by ROMS flow fields), so it is a concrete example of closing the loop between particle tracking and what is actually found on beaches.
- **It is reproducible.** The deposit includes a reproduction manifest with a checksum checker, and the full particle trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are available on request — useful if you want to benchmark your own setup against theirs.

One caveat: I could not read the project's confirmed state (goals, method, blockers) for #2 in this conversation, so I am judging fit from the project's name and the slate alone. If the team has a specific open blocker — say, a beaching parameterisation or a validation dataset — #4 is the item to pull first; if the blocker is elsewhere, the ranking may shift. You can confirm or update the project's state in the app.

A practical next step: have Jonah or Priya read #4's README and kernel code to see whether the OceanParcels beaching kernel can be dropped into your existing particle-tracking setup, and request the ROMS flow fields if you want to compare against their Uido case.

final_text:
Here's the comparison.

**#1 – Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This call is about strengthening the *infrastructure* of global ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing system experiments, network optimization, and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (deep sea, polar). It's framed around EU strategic autonomy, GOOS governance, and biodiversity monitoring. The emphasis is on *building and sustaining the observing network itself*, not on developing forecasting methods.

**#2 – Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This call is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Southern Ocean: ocean–ice–atmosphere interactions, decadal-to-millennial climate projections, extreme events, tipping points, and ecosystem vulnerability. It explicitly asks for improved projections, monitoring indicators, and Earth System Model enhancement. The emphasis is on *science of change and prediction* in a specific region.

**Fit with the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3):**

The project's core is *forecasting* marine heatwaves using ocean models, satellite data, and machine learning, and delivering those forecasts to coastal managers. The lab's stated method is "combine ocean models, satellite observations and machine learning to forecast what coastal waters will do next."

- **#2 fits better on the science side.** It asks for improved projections, extreme events, and monitoring indicators — which is closer to what the project actually does (predicting marine heatwaves, evaluating forecasts, building early-warning capability). The project's slate already includes papers on ML-based MHW forecasting (#8) and forecast-triggered rapid response (#7), which align with #2's interest in extreme events and decision-relevant projections.

- **#1 fits less well.** It's primarily an infrastructure and governance call. While the project *uses* observations (satellite, in-situ), it doesn't aim to deploy new equipment, optimize observing networks, or strengthen GOOS governance. The project's contribution to #1 would be thin — you'd be a consumer of the observing system, not a builder of it.

**Biggest doubt on #2:** the call is regionally specific (Antarctica / Southern Ocean), while the project is a *lab* project with a broader coastal focus. If the project's current work is on temperate or tropical coastal waters, you'd need to reframe it toward the Southern Ocean to be competitive. That's a real constraint.

**Biggest doubt on #1:** the €50M scale and the infrastructure focus suggest a large consortium with hardware deployment. A 3-person lab project focused on ML forecasting would be a small piece of that, and the call's expected outcomes (equipment deployment, network optimization, EU strategic autonomy) are not what the project is built to deliver.

**Bottom line:** #2 is the better fit for the project's *science* (prediction, extremes, monitoring), but you'd need to anchor the proposal in the Southern Ocean region. #1 is a bigger pot of money but asks for something the project isn't structured to do (build observing infrastructure). If the project has any Southern Ocean component or can credibly extend there, #2 is the stronger target.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Two grants are open on the project's slate, and #9 is the stronger fit:

It asks for proposals that "stabilise, further strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system." - **#4 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination** (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15). This is an *instrumentation-development* program. No one in the lab declares instrumentation development, so it's a weaker fit for a forecasting/assimilation project.

So **#9 is the best fit**, and it's also the bigger, more strategic prize.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Here's what I found.

## Best fit: #4 Microplastics Research and Resource Coordination Center (U24)

Of the open calls I checked, #4 is the clearest match for Plastic pathways. It funds a coordination center to standardize sampling and analytical methods, harmonize data, and distribute experimental standards across the micro/nanoplastics research community — which is exactly the kind of infrastructure a pathways project needs to make its data comparable across studies. It's still open, with a deadline of **2026-12-01** — about three weeks away, so this is the one to move on quickly.

The others fit less well:
- **#3** (biotech recycling of complex plastics) is about industrial recycling technology, not environmental pathways.
- **#7** (seafood supply chain circularity) and **#8** (green harbours) are about waste valorisation and port management, not plastic transport in the ocean.
- **#9** (waterborne transport impacts) is about zero-carbon fuel spills, a different pollution problem.

One honest caveat: #4 is an NIH U24 mechanism, which typically requires a US institution, and its emphasis is on health effects of M/NPs — I can't see your institution's country or whether the project has a health-effects angle, so check eligibility before committing.

## Who should lead

**Jonah Whitcombe (#15)** is the natural lead: he's a project member and his declared interests are marine litter and Lagrangian analysis — the core of Plastic pathways.

**Priya Raman (#16)** is the strongest co-lead: satellite oceanography and coastal water quality map directly onto the call's sampling, monitoring and data-harmonization slots.

**You** would anchor it as PI. But be aware of the gap: Mylo's slot check for #4 found no lab member whose declared profile covers the health-effects or analytical-standardization slots, so the application would need to lean on your group's environmental pathways expertise and frame the health-effects piece as a collaboration.

## Partners outside the lab

I can't name any: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I have no consented people to suggest. What I can say from the call itself is that a U24 center proposal expects a multidisciplinary consortium — you'd want at least one group with M/NP analytical/health-effects expertise, since that's the slot no one in the lab covers. You can look for those partners in the app.

Want me to pull the project's current slate and blockers (#2) to see what's already in motion before the 1 December deadline?

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new and where the money could come from.

## Where the project stands

The project is a lab-scoped effort with three members: Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. I can see the membership, but the project's confirmed state — goals, method, blockers, milestones — isn't recorded in Mycelium, so I can't tell you how far along it is or what's blocking it. If the team has confirmed a state in the app, it isn't visible to me here.

## Three most relevant new papers

From the project's current slate, the three that speak most directly to plastic pathways:

1. **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). A three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. This is the closest match: it's a particle-tracking method for where marine litter ends up, with code and aggregated results available.
2. **#12 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). A YOLO11-based framework for detecting low-contrast, curved features in satellite imagery. Relevant as a method template: automated satellite detection of hard-to-see ocean features, which could transfer to debris detection from space.
3. **#6 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). A data release of daily analyses from a regional ocean forecast system. Relevant as a potential flow-field source for particle tracking, though I can only see the title and deposit details — no abstract or method reading is available for this one, so treat this as the weakest of the three.

The other new papers on the slate (#5 LiDAR phytoplankton, #9 a comment, #11 multi-agent tracking) are further afield.

## One funding opportunity

**#10 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC), NSF.** This program supports unsolicited proposals for instrumentation development that enhances observational, experimental, or analytical capabilities for the ocean science community. It fits Plastic pathways well: the lab's statement (#13) is built on combining ocean models, satellite observations and ML to track where floating debris ends up, and a proposal developing new observational or analytical capability for debris tracking would sit squarely in OTIC's scope. The deadline is **2027-02-15** and it is still open.

The biggest doubt: OTIC leans toward *technology and instrumentation development*, so the strongest framing would be a new method or tool (e.g., a satellite-based debris detection pipeline or a novel particle-tracking kernel) rather than a pure modelling study. I can't see the full eligibility rules or budget requirements from here, so check the program description (PD-98-1680) before committing.

A larger alternative on the slate is **#3** (€50M, EU, deadline 2027-02-16), but it's aimed at strengthening the global observing system and biodiversity observation — a broader, more infrastructure-oriented fit than what Plastic pathways appears to be doing.

If you'd like, I can dig into any of these papers in full, or look at who in the lab might lead an OTIC application.

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#35 [paper] Code and aggregated results for "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"
Authors: Sehan Lim, Sunwook Hong
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24075707
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Development and application of a tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter tracking.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A three-phase beaching kernel and six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, along with scripts for particle-tracking experiments and result aggregation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Field records from Uido, Republic of Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories.
Abstract:
Code and aggregated results accompanying the manuscript "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea" (submitted to Marine Pollution Bulletin). The deposit contains:- kernel/kernels.py: the three-phase beaching kernel and six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4 (also uploaded separately as kernels.py);- the scripts that ran the particle-tracking experiments and aggregated their output;- the aggregated result files from which every number in the manuscript was taken;- the reproduction record (repro/manifest.json) with its checker. Particle trajectories (about 32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (about 37 GB) are available on request. See README.md for the contents and for verification (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS).
